title: Chapter 6: Tool-Using Agents in Python
content:
Chapter 6: Tool-Using Agents in Python

Opening Hook: From Talking About Work to Doing Work

A chatbot can talk about a calculation.

A tool-using agent can actually calculate.

A chatbot can explain what an API is.

A tool-using agent can call an API.

A chatbot can tell you how to summarize text.

A tool-using agent can take the text, run the right function, and return the summary.

This is the chapter where your AI assistant starts to feel more like an agent.

So far, your projects have mostly focused on understanding, generating, and retrieving text.

You built:

  • A code explainer
  • A reusable LLM client
  • A command-line assistant
  • A PDF RAG assistant
  • A semantic search engine

Now you will add a new ability:

Tools.

A tool is a Python function your agent can use.

That simple idea changes everything.

Instead of relying only on the model, your app can combine model reasoning with actual software actions.

In this chapter, you will build your second flagship project:

API Tool-Using Agent

It will choose from a small set of tools, run the selected tool, and then use the LLM to explain the result clearly.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • What tool calling means
  • Why tools make AI agents more useful
  • How Python functions become agent tools
  • How to design safe tool inputs
  • How to build a tool router
  • How to create calculator, summarizer, and API tools
  • How to validate tool names and tool inputs
  • How to log tool calls
  • Why unrestricted tools are dangerous
  • How this pattern connects to production agent frameworks

Why This Chapter Matters

An AI model is powerful, but it has limits.

It may not know live data.

It may make math mistakes.

It cannot safely access your private APIs unless your app gives it controlled access.

It cannot update databases, send emails, or check files by itself.

Tools solve part of this problem.

A tool gives your agent a controlled way to interact with software.

For example:

User RequestTool Needed
“What is 245 × 18?”Calculator
“Summarize this paragraph.”Summarizer
“What is my public IP?”API lookup
“Find notes about RAG.”Semantic search
“Search this PDF.”RAG retriever
“Create a task list.”Task planner

Modern AI APIs and agent frameworks support tool calling patterns, but the core idea is simple:

The model can help decide what action is needed, and your application controls which tool actually runs.

In this chapter, you will build that control layer yourself.

Framework magic is easier to understand after you know the underlying pattern.

6.1 What Is a Tool?

A tool is a function that performs one clear action.

Example:

def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int: return a + b

For an AI agent, a tool might be:

def calculator(expression: str) -> str: ...

or:

def summarize_text(text: str) -> str: ...

or:

def get_public_ip(_: str = "") -> str: ...

The model does not directly control your computer.

Your Python app controls the tools.

That distinction is important.

A safe tool-using agent should follow this pattern:

User request ↓ Tool selection ↓ Input validation ↓ Tool execution ↓ Tool result ↓ Final response

The model may help select a tool, but your code decides what tools exist, what inputs are allowed, and what result is returned.

6.2 Why Tools Matter

Without tools, an LLM can only generate text.

With tools, your app can:

  • Calculate
  • Search
  • Retrieve documents
  • Query APIs
  • Read files
  • Format data
  • Create reports
  • Trigger workflows
  • Ask for human approval before actions

Tools turn an AI assistant from a text generator into a task helper.

But tools also introduce risk.

A poorly designed tool can:

  • Leak private data
  • Delete important files
  • Send unwanted emails
  • Make expensive API calls
  • Run unsafe code
  • Produce wrong results
  • Take actions without approval

So the goal is not:

Give the AI every tool.

The goal is:

Give the agent narrow, safe, useful tools with clear rules.

6.3 Tool Calling vs Function Calling

You may see two common phrases:

  • Tool calling
  • Function calling

In many AI development conversations, these ideas are closely related.

A function is a piece of code.

A tool is a function exposed to an AI system in a controlled way.

For example, this is a regular function:

def word_count(text: str) -> int: return len(text.split())

It becomes an agent tool when your app allows the AI workflow to choose and run it.

A tool usually needs:

  • A name
  • A description
  • Input rules
  • Output format
  • Safety limits

In beginner projects, you can build a manual tool router.

In advanced projects, you can use provider-supported tool calling or an agent framework.

This chapter uses a manual router first.

That keeps the logic visible.

6.4 The Manual Tool Router Pattern

A manual tool router asks the model to choose a tool from an approved list.

The model returns structured text, usually JSON.

Your Python app parses the JSON, checks whether the tool is allowed, runs the tool, and returns the result.

The flow looks like this:

User request ↓ LLM chooses tool from approved list ↓ Python validates tool choice ↓ Python runs the tool ↓ Tool result returns to app ↓ LLM writes final answer

Important:

The model suggests. Your code decides.

This prevents the model from inventing tools or running unsafe actions.

6.5 Project: API Tool-Using Agent

What This Project Does

This project builds an agent that can use three tools:

  1. Calculator tool
  2. Text summarizer tool
  3. Public IP lookup API tool

The user can type:

What is 245 * 18?

The agent chooses the calculator tool.

The user can type:

Summarize this: Python is used for automation, AI, and web development.

The agent chooses the summarizer tool.

The user can type:

What is my public IP?

The agent chooses the API lookup tool.

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Python learners understand tool calling
  • Developers build safer AI assistants
  • Freelancers prototype business automation tools
  • Students create stronger portfolio projects
  • Future chapters that need tools, workflows, and guardrails

What You Will Build

Create this project structure:

chapter_06_tool_agent/ tools/ __init__.py calculator.py api_tools.py summarizer.py .env.example .gitignore requirements.txt llm_client.py tool_registry.py tool_router.py agent.py app.py test_calculator.py test_tool_registry.py test_tool_router.py README.md

6.6 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_06_tool_agent cd chapter_06_tool_agent mkdir tools

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai python-dotenv pytest requests

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

6.7 File: .gitignore

Create .gitignore:

.env .venv/ __pycache__/ .pytest_cache/ *.pyc *.log

6.8 File: tools/init.py

Create tools/__init__.py:

""" Tool package for Chapter 6. """ Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

This makes the tools folder importable as a Python package.

6.9 File: llm_client.py

Create llm_client.py:

""" Chapter 6: Reusable LLM Client """ import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI load_dotenv() def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float: """Read a float from environment variables safely.""" raw_value = os.getenv(name) if raw_value is None: return default try: return float(raw_value) except ValueError: return default @dataclass class LLMConfig: """Configuration for the LLM client.""" model: str = field( default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini") ) temperature: float = field( default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2) ) class LLMClient: """Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM.""" def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None): self.config = config or LLMConfig() api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY") if not api_key: raise ValueError( "OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file." ) self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key) def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str: """Send a request to the model and return text output.""" if not system.strip(): raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.") if not user.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") model_input = f""" System instruction: {system.strip()} User request: {user.strip()} """ response = self.client.responses.create( model=self.config.model, input=model_input, temperature=self.config.temperature, ) return response.output_text Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

6.10 File: tools/calculator.py

A calculator tool sounds simple, but it can be dangerous if implemented badly.

Many beginners write this:

eval(user_input)

That is risky.

eval() can execute arbitrary Python code if user input is malicious.

For this project, you will build a safer calculator using Python’s ast module.

Create tools/calculator.py:

""" Safe calculator tool for the Chapter 6 tool-using agent. This tool supports: - Addition - Subtraction - Multiplication - Division - Exponents - Parentheses - Unary plus and minus It does not execute arbitrary Python code. """ import ast import operator ALLOWED_OPERATORS = { ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul, ast.Div: operator.truediv, ast.Pow: operator.pow, ast.USub: operator.neg, ast.UAdd: operator.pos, } def evaluate_node(node): """Recursively evaluate a safe arithmetic AST node.""" if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)): return node.value if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp): left = evaluate_node(node.left) right = evaluate_node(node.right) operator_type = type(node.op) if operator_type not in ALLOWED_OPERATORS: raise ValueError("Unsupported arithmetic operator.") return ALLOWED_OPERATORS[operator_type](left, right) if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp): operand = evaluate_node(node.operand) operator_type = type(node.op) if operator_type not in ALLOWED_OPERATORS: raise ValueError("Unsupported unary operator.") return ALLOWED_OPERATORS[operator_type](operand) raise ValueError("Unsupported expression.") def calculator(expression: str) -> str: """ Evaluate a basic arithmetic expression safely. Args: expression: Arithmetic expression as text. Returns: The calculated result as a string. """ if not expression.strip(): return "Calculator error: expression cannot be empty." if len(expression) > 200: return "Calculator error: expression is too long." try: parsed = ast.parse(expression, mode="eval") result = evaluate_node(parsed.body) return str(result) except ZeroDivisionError: return "Calculator error: division by zero." except Exception as error: return f"Calculator error: {error}" Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.11 File: tools/api_tools.py

This file contains a simple public API lookup tool.

Create tools/api_tools.py:

""" API tools for the Chapter 6 tool-using agent. """ import requests def get_public_ip(_: str = "") -> str: """ Fetch the public IP address using a simple public API. The input argument is ignored so the tool has a consistent signature. """ url = "https://api.ipify.org?format=json" try: response = requests.get(url, timeout=10) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() ip_address = data.get("ip") if not ip_address: return "API error: response did not include an IP address." return f"Public IP address: {ip_address}" except requests.Timeout: return "API error: request timed out." except requests.RequestException as error: return f"API error: {error}" except ValueError: return "API error: response was not valid JSON." Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

External API calls should use timeouts so your app does not wait forever if a service is slow or unavailable.

6.12 File: tools/summarizer.py

The summarizer tool uses the LLM client.

This is a tool that calls the model again.

That is allowed, but remember that each model call can affect cost and latency.

Create tools/summarizer.py:

""" Text summarizer tool for the Chapter 6 tool-using agent. """ from llm_client import LLMClient def summarize_text(text: str) -> str: """ Summarize text in three bullet points. """ if not text.strip(): return "Summarizer error: text cannot be empty." if len(text) > 5000: return "Summarizer error: text is too long for this beginner demo." client = LLMClient() return client.complete( system="You summarize text clearly and accurately.", user=f""" Summarize the following text in three bullet points. Text: {text} Rules: - Do not add facts that are not present. - Keep the summary concise. """, ) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.13 File: tool_registry.py

The tool registry is a list of approved tools.

This is important.

The agent should not be able to call any Python function.

It should only call tools you approve.

Create tool_registry.py:

""" Tool registry for the Chapter 6 tool-using agent. """ from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable from tools.calculator import calculator from tools.api_tools import get_public_ip from tools.summarizer import summarize_text ToolFunction = Callable[[str], str] @dataclass class Tool: """A tool the agent is allowed to use.""" name: str description: str function: ToolFunction TOOLS: dict[str, Tool] = { "calculator": Tool( name="calculator", description="Use for basic arithmetic expressions such as 245 * 18.", function=calculator, ), "summarize_text": Tool( name="summarize_text", description="Use for summarizing user-provided text.", function=summarize_text, ), "get_public_ip": Tool( name="get_public_ip", description="Use when the user asks for the public IP address.", function=get_public_ip, ), } def get_tool_descriptions() -> str: """ Return tool descriptions for the router prompt. """ lines = [] for tool in TOOLS.values(): lines.append(f"- {tool.name}: {tool.description}") return "\n".join(lines) def is_allowed_tool(tool_name: str) -> bool: """ Check whether the requested tool is approved. """ return tool_name in TOOLS def run_tool(tool_name: str, tool_input: str) -> str: """ Run an approved tool. """ if not is_allowed_tool(tool_name): return f"Tool error: '{tool_name}' is not an allowed tool." tool = TOOLS[tool_name] return tool.function(tool_input) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.14 File: tool_router.py

This file asks the model to choose the best tool.

The model must return JSON.

Then your Python code parses and validates it.

Create tool_router.py:

""" Tool router for the Chapter 6 tool-using agent. The router asks the LLM to choose one approved tool. """ import json from dataclasses import dataclass from llm_client import LLMClient from tool_registry import get_tool_descriptions, is_allowed_tool ROUTER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a tool router for a Python AI agent. Your job is to choose the best tool for the user's request. You must choose only from the approved tools. Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown. Do not explain your decision outside JSON. """ @dataclass class ToolDecision: """The tool chosen by the router.""" tool_name: str tool_input: str reason: str def build_router_prompt(user_request: str) -> str: """ Build a prompt asking the model to choose a tool. """ tool_descriptions = get_tool_descriptions() return f""" Approved tools: {tool_descriptions} User request: {user_request} Return only JSON with this structure: {{ "tool_name": "calculator | summarize_text | get_public_ip", "tool_input": "input to pass to the tool", "reason": "short reason for choosing this tool" }} Rules: - Use calculator only for arithmetic. - Use summarize_text only when the user asks to summarize text. - Use get_public_ip only when the user asks for public IP. - If the request contains arithmetic, tool_input should be only the expression. - If the request asks for summarization, tool_input should be the text to summarize. - If the request asks for public IP, tool_input can be an empty string. """ def parse_tool_decision(raw_text: str) -> ToolDecision: """ Parse the router's JSON output into a ToolDecision. """ try: data = json.loads(raw_text) except json.JSONDecodeError as error: raise ValueError(f"Router did not return valid JSON: {error}") from error tool_name = str(data.get("tool_name", "")).strip() tool_input = str(data.get("tool_input", "")).strip() reason = str(data.get("reason", "")).strip() if not tool_name: raise ValueError("Router response is missing tool_name.") if not is_allowed_tool(tool_name): raise ValueError(f"Router chose an unsupported tool: {tool_name}") return ToolDecision( tool_name=tool_name, tool_input=tool_input, reason=reason or "No reason provided.", ) def choose_tool(user_request: str) -> ToolDecision: """ Ask the LLM to choose a tool for the user request. """ if not user_request.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") client = LLMClient() prompt = build_router_prompt(user_request) raw_response = client.complete( system=ROUTER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=prompt, ) return parse_tool_decision(raw_response) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.15 File: agent.py

The agent combines everything.

It:

  1. Receives a user request
  2. Chooses a tool
  3. Runs the tool
  4. Sends the tool result back to the LLM
  5. Returns a final answer

Create agent.py:

""" Tool-using agent for Chapter 6. """ from llm_client import LLMClient from tool_registry import run_tool from tool_router import choose_tool, ToolDecision FINAL_ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a practical AI assistant. You receive: 1. The user's original request 2. The tool that was used 3. The tool result Write a clear final answer for the user. Rules: - Do not invent tool results. - If the tool returned an error, explain it simply. - Keep the answer concise. """ def build_final_answer_prompt( user_request: str, decision: ToolDecision, tool_result: str, ) -> str: """ Build the prompt for the final user-facing answer. """ return f""" User request: {user_request} Tool selected: {decision.tool_name} Router reason: {decision.reason} Tool input: {decision.tool_input} Tool result: {tool_result} Write the final answer for the user. """ def run_agent(user_request: str) -> str: """ Run the full tool-using agent workflow. """ if not user_request.strip(): return "Please enter a request." try: decision = choose_tool(user_request) except Exception as error: return f"Tool routing error: {error}" tool_result = run_tool( tool_name=decision.tool_name, tool_input=decision.tool_input, ) try: client = LLMClient() final_prompt = build_final_answer_prompt( user_request=user_request, decision=decision, tool_result=tool_result, ) return client.complete( system=FINAL_ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=final_prompt, ) except Exception as error: return ( "The tool ran, but the final explanation failed.\n" f"Tool used: {decision.tool_name}\n" f"Tool result: {tool_result}\n" f"Explanation error: {error}" ) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.16 File: app.py

This is the command-line interface.

Create app.py:

""" Chapter 6 Project: API Tool-Using Agent """ from agent import run_agent def main() -> None: """Run the command-line tool-using agent.""" print("\nAPI Tool-Using Agent") print("=" * 40) print("Ask for calculations, summaries, or your public IP.") print("Type /exit to quit.") print("=" * 40) while True: user_request = input("\nRequest: ").strip() if user_request.lower() in {"/exit", "exit", "quit"}: print("Goodbye.") break if not user_request: print("Please enter a request.") continue answer = run_agent(user_request) print("\nAgent:") print(answer) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.17 File: test_calculator.py

These tests validate the calculator without calling the model API.

Create test_calculator.py:

from tools.calculator import calculator def test_calculator_addition(): assert calculator("2 + 3") == "5" def test_calculator_multiplication(): assert calculator("6 * 7") == "42" def test_calculator_parentheses(): assert calculator("(2 + 3) * 4") == "20" def test_calculator_division_by_zero(): result = calculator("10 / 0") assert "division by zero" in result def test_calculator_rejects_unsupported_expression(): result = calculator("__import__('os').system('echo unsafe')") assert "Calculator error" in result def test_calculator_empty_expression(): result = calculator("") assert "cannot be empty" in result Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.18 File: test_tool_registry.py

Create test_tool_registry.py:

from tool_registry import ( TOOLS, get_tool_descriptions, is_allowed_tool, run_tool, ) def test_tool_registry_contains_expected_tools(): assert "calculator" in TOOLS assert "summarize_text" in TOOLS assert "get_public_ip" in TOOLS def test_get_tool_descriptions_mentions_tools(): descriptions = get_tool_descriptions() assert "calculator" in descriptions assert "summarize_text" in descriptions assert "get_public_ip" in descriptions def test_is_allowed_tool(): assert is_allowed_tool("calculator") is True assert is_allowed_tool("delete_files") is False def test_run_allowed_calculator_tool(): result = run_tool("calculator", "10 + 5") assert result == "15" def test_run_disallowed_tool(): result = run_tool("delete_files", "anything") assert "not an allowed tool" in result Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.19 File: test_tool_router.py

These tests check router prompt building and JSON parsing without making an API call.

Create test_tool_router.py:

import pytest from tool_router import ( build_router_prompt, parse_tool_decision, ) def test_build_router_prompt_includes_user_request(): prompt = build_router_prompt("What is 2 + 2?") assert "What is 2 + 2?" in prompt assert "Approved tools:" in prompt assert "calculator" in prompt def test_parse_tool_decision_valid_json(): raw = """ { "tool_name": "calculator", "tool_input": "2 + 2", "reason": "The user asked for arithmetic." } """ decision = parse_tool_decision(raw) assert decision.tool_name == "calculator" assert decision.tool_input == "2 + 2" assert "arithmetic" in decision.reason def test_parse_tool_decision_invalid_json(): with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse_tool_decision("not json") def test_parse_tool_decision_rejects_unknown_tool(): raw = """ { "tool_name": "delete_files", "tool_input": "/", "reason": "Unsafe request." } """ with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse_tool_decision(raw) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

6.21 How the Code Works

This project has five major parts.

Part 1: Tools

Each tool is a normal Python function.

For example:

calculator("245 * 18")

returns:

4410

The agent does not magically know how to calculate.

It uses your Python calculator tool.

Part 2: Tool Registry

The registry defines which tools are allowed.

TOOLS = { "calculator": Tool(...), "summarize_text": Tool(...), "get_public_ip": Tool(...), }

This is important because the model should not be able to invent dangerous tools.

If the model tries to choose:

delete_files

your app rejects it.

Part 3: Tool Router

The router asks the LLM to choose one approved tool.

It returns JSON like this:

{ "tool_name": "calculator", "tool_input": "245 * 18", "reason": "The user asked for arithmetic." }

Then your code parses and validates the JSON.

Part 4: Tool Execution

After validation, the app runs:

tool_result = run_tool( tool_name=decision.tool_name, tool_input=decision.tool_input, )

The tool result is plain text.

Part 5: Final Answer

The app sends the tool result back to the LLM and asks for a clear final answer.

This makes the response friendlier.

Instead of showing only:

4410

the assistant can say:

245 × 18 = 4410.

6.22 Sample User Session

A typical session may look like this:

API Tool-Using Agent ======================================== Ask for calculations, summaries, or your public IP. Type /exit to quit. ======================================== Request: What is 245 * 18? Agent: 245 × 18 = 4410.

Another example:

Request: Summarize this: Python is popular because it is readable, flexible, and has a large ecosystem for AI, automation, and web development. Agent: Here is a concise summary: - Python is popular because it is readable and beginner-friendly. - It is flexible enough for AI, automation, and web development. - Its large ecosystem makes it practical for many real-world projects.

Another example:

Request: What is my public IP? Agent: Your public IP address is: 203.0.113.10

This is sample output only.

Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result.

6.23 Testing the Project

Run:

pytest

Expected type of result:

15 passed

The exact number and timing may vary if you add more tests.

These tests check:

  • Calculator behavior
  • Rejection of unsafe expressions
  • Tool registry contents
  • Disallowed tool handling
  • Router prompt creation
  • Router JSON parsing
  • Unsupported tool rejection

Most tests do not call the LLM.

That is intentional.

A good AI app separates normal Python logic from live model calls.

6.24 Live API Testing

After adding your API key to .env, run:

python app.py

Try:

What is 88 * 12? Summarize this: AI agents combine models, tools, memory, and control logic. What is my public IP?

Also test a confusing or unsafe request:

Can you delete all my files?

In this beginner version, no delete tool exists in the registry.

Since no delete tool exists, the app cannot delete files.

This is the point of the registry.

The agent can only use approved tools.

6.25 Debugging Tool-Using Agents

Tool-using agents can fail in several ways.

ProblemLikely CauseFix
Wrong tool selectedRouter prompt is unclearImprove tool descriptions
JSON parse errorModel returned extra textStrengthen “return only JSON” rule
Tool input is messyRouter did not extract input cleanlyAdd examples to router prompt
Tool failsBad input or external API issueAdd validation and error handling
Final answer invents detailsFinal prompt too looseTell model to use only tool result
App is slowToo many LLM callsReduce calls or cache
API call hangsNo timeoutAdd request timeout

When debugging, inspect:

  • User request
  • Router raw response
  • Parsed tool decision
  • Tool input
  • Tool result
  • Final answer prompt

Do not hide the intermediate steps while building.

Agents become easier to improve when you can see each step.

6.26 Why Not Let the Model Run Any Code?

A common beginner mistake is to give the model a tool that runs arbitrary Python.

That is dangerous.

For example:

eval(user_input)

can become unsafe if user input contains malicious code.

A tool-using agent should not have unlimited power.

Instead:

  • Use narrow tools
  • Validate inputs
  • Use allowlists
  • Add human approval
  • Log tool calls
  • Avoid destructive actions
  • Avoid unrestricted file access
  • Avoid arbitrary code execution

The calculator in this chapter uses Python’s ast module to allow only basic arithmetic.

That is safer than unrestricted eval().

6.27 Tool Safety Rules

Use these rules when designing tools.

Rule 1: One Tool, One Job

A tool should do one clear thing.

Good:

calculate arithmetic expression

Risky:

run any Python command

Rule 2: Validate Inputs

Check for empty, long, malformed, or risky input.

Rule 3: Limit Permissions

A tool should only access what it needs.

Rule 4: Add Timeouts

External API calls should not wait forever.

Rule 5: Log Important Actions

Keep a record of what tools were called.

Rule 6: Require Human Approval for Risky Actions

Human review should be required before:

  • Sending emails
  • Making purchases
  • Deleting data
  • Updating records
  • Sharing private information
  • Triggering financial actions

Rule 7: Return Clear Errors

A failed tool should not crash the whole app.

It should return a clear message.

6.28 Adding Simple Tool Logs

You can add a basic logger.

Create tool_logger.py:

""" Simple tool logging utility. """ from datetime import datetime def log_tool_call(tool_name: str, tool_input: str, tool_result: str) -> None: """ Save a tool call record to a local log file. Do not log secrets or sensitive private data in production systems. """ with open("tool_calls.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file: file.write(f"{datetime.now().isoformat()}\n") file.write(f"Tool: {tool_name}\n") file.write(f"Input: {tool_input[:500]}\n") file.write(f"Result: {tool_result[:500]}\n") file.write("-" * 60 + "\n") Test result: Python syntax check passed.

Then update agent.py:

from tool_logger import log_tool_call

After running the tool:

log_tool_call( tool_name=decision.tool_name, tool_input=decision.tool_input, tool_result=tool_result, )

This is useful for debugging.

For production systems, logs must be designed carefully to avoid storing sensitive information.

6.31 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Giving the Agent Dangerous Tools

Do not give a beginner agent tools like:

delete_file send_payment run_shell_command email_client update_database

unless you have strict validation and human approval.

Mistake 2: Trusting the Router Completely

The model can choose the wrong tool.

Always validate the tool name.

Mistake 3: Not Validating Tool Input

Bad input creates bad tool results.

Check for empty input, length, format, and risky patterns.

Mistake 4: Using Unrestricted eval

Avoid:

eval(user_input)

Use safer alternatives.

Mistake 5: Hiding Intermediate Steps

While developing, inspect:

  • Router response
  • Parsed decision
  • Tool input
  • Tool result

Mistake 6: Forgetting Timeouts

External APIs may be slow or unavailable.

Use timeouts and handle errors.

Mistake 7: Automating Without Approval

A tool that sends emails, deletes files, updates records, or makes purchases should require human review.

6.32 Best Practices

Keep tools narrow.

Use a tool registry.

Validate tool names.

Validate tool inputs.

Return clear errors.

Set API timeouts.

Log tool calls carefully.

Do not give unrestricted file, shell, or database access.

Use human approval for risky actions.

Test tools independently before connecting them to an agent.

Start with read-only tools before adding write actions.
